title: Why It Makes Sense to Factor All of Your Loads
summary: Do you have to factor every load? Learn why factoring all your loads gives owner-operators and small fleets steadier cash flow and simpler operations.

You delivered the load. The work's done. But the broker won't pay for 30, 45, or even 60 days.


Meanwhile, fuel, insurance, truck payments, and payroll keep coming.


That gap between finishing the job and getting paid is where a lot of carriers get stuck. It's also why so many owner-operators and small fleets use freight factoring.


One question comes up early: Do you have to factor every load, or can you factor only certain loads? It's a fair question. For most carriers there's a better one to ask: What do you gain when you factor all of your loads?


Before deciding on your factoring relationship, it helps to understand:


- Why factoring all loads can help create a more predictable cash flow for many carriers


- How one process simplifies your back office


- How to handle common concerns about fees and contracts


- What to look for in your factoring agreement


## **Should You Factor All of Your Loads?**


For many carriers, factoring all loads can help create a more predictable cash flow and a consistent process. It also keeps every broker on a similar payment timeline.


Factoring agreement terms vary by provider and by broker. Many agreements are built around submitting all eligible invoices. That's why it's important to understand your contract before you make any decisions.


## **The Real Problem Is Timing, Not Profit**


Many loads are profitable on paper. The trouble is when the money shows up.


Most brokers pay on net-30 to net-45 terms, and some take longer. Some industry terms stretch to 60 or even 90 days. That's up to three months of waiting after you've already done the work.


Those delays create pressure across your whole operation:


- **Fuel:** Fuel is often your largest variable expense, at roughly 25% to 35% of operating costs.


- **Drivers:** Driver pay doesn't wait for a broker's payment cycle.


- **Maintenance:** Repairs get pushed back when cash is tight.


- **Growth:** Adding trucks or drivers takes working capital you can't access yet.


Here's the key: Cash flow problems hit new carriers hardest. Many new owner-operators run low on cash in their first 90 days. It's not because they aren't earning. It's because they're waiting to get paid.


## **Why Factoring More of Your Loads Can Help Smooth Out Cash Flow**


When you factor every load, you can create a more consistent flow of cash from approved invoices. You're not guessing which invoices will pay this week and which will drag on.


Compare the two approaches:


- **Factoring only certain loads:** Some invoices get funded fast. Others sit for 30 to 60 days. Your bank balance swings week to week.


- **Factoring all loads:** Factoring approved invoices can give you better visibility into when cash is coming in, based on your funding process and agreement.


That consistency matters because your biggest costs run on their own schedule. Fuel, insurance, and truck payments don't care which loads you factored.


### **Example: A Two-Truck Operation**


Say you run two trucks and haul four loads a week. You factor two and wait on the other two. Then a repair bill lands during that gap. Now you're scrambling.


Factor all four, and the cash from each load keeps flowing. That repair becomes a cost you can handle, not a crisis.


## **One Process for Every Invoice**


Factoring only some loads means running two systems. One set of invoices goes to your factoring company. The other goes straight to brokers, and you're the one chasing payment.


That adds work you don't need:


- Tracking which loads went where


- Making collection calls on late payments


- Keeping separate records for factored and unfactored invoices


- Deciding, load by load, which invoices to factor


Factoring all loads replaces that with one routine. Haul, submit your paperwork, and get paid. Your factoring company handles collections. You get more time to drive, book freight, and run your business.


## **Broker Credit Checks on Every Load**


Some factoring companies provide broker credit information that can help you evaluate who you haul for before you book a load.


That can give you another data point when deciding who you want to haul for. That extra information can help you make more informed decisions about who you haul for. This matters most in your first months of authority, while you're still learning which brokers pay on time.


It also helps your broker relationships. Brokers know exactly where to send payment. That means fewer misdirected payments and fewer awkward calls about who's supposed to get paid.


## **Room to Grow or Maintain Your Fleet**


Steady cash flow makes growth and maintenance decisions easier. When money comes in on a schedule you can count on, you can:


- **Add a truck** without draining your savings


- **Hire a driver** and know you can cover payroll


- **Take on new lanes** without waiting weeks to recover costs


- **Plan for insurance increases** as your fleet expands


- **Build a cash cushion** for slow seasons


Small fleets can grow fast if they build solid broker relationships. The more loads you run, the more consistent factoring process pays off. One system scales with you and has dedicated team members to support different parts of your business: broker credit checks, invoicing, account resolutions, broker relationships and more.


Managing all of that as an owner is possible, but it limits your ability to focus on building your business, and it doesn’t let you take advantage of the experience that a factoring company has in doing these tasks every day.


## **Why Factoring Agreements Usually Cover All Your Invoices**


Many factoring agreements include exclusivity provisions, though terms vary by provider.


In plain terms, the lien shows that your factoring company has a right to the invoices in your agreement. That's why carriers generally can't work with two factoring companies at once.


This is one more reason factoring all your loads makes sense. Your agreement is already set up around one company handling your invoices. Working within that structure keeps things clean for you, your factoring company, and your brokers.


**Watch for this:** Every contract is different. Before you sign or make changes, know your:


- Advance rate and factoring fee


- Reserve amount, if any


- Minimum volume requirements


- Contract length and termination terms


- Recourse or non-recourse coverage


## **Common Concerns About Factoring All Loads**


### **"Won't I Pay More in Fees?"**


Factoring more loads means more invoices carry a fee. But payment delays have costs too: missed loads, downtime, emergency repairs, driver turnover, and interest on credit cards or loans.


Look at your total cost, not just the headline rate. Ask about wire fees, invoice processing fees, and reserves.


Remember, in a factoring relationship you are getting more than just faster access to your payments; you’re getting a team that works on different parts of the business at a fraction of what hiring people would cost.


**Look at the cost of factoring against the benefits.** Factoring fees are a cost of doing business and may be tax deductible. When weighing the fee, consider it alongside the cash flow and back-office benefits factoring provides.


### **"Can't I Just Factor Only Certain Loads to Save Money?"**


It can look that way. But factoring only certain loads often means higher per-invoice rates, uneven cash flow, and more time spent on collections. The savings can disappear fast when you count your time and the cost of waiting.


### **"What If a Broker Pays Fast Anyway?"**


Even fast-paying brokers can slow down. Running every load through one process protects you from surprises. You also get consistent pricing across all loads, which makes costs easier to predict.


### **"Will I Lose Control of My Invoices?"**


You stay in control of your business. What you hand off is the invoicing, follow-up calls, and collections. That frees up hours you can spend hauling more loads.


### **"What About Long-Term Contracts?"**


This is a fair concern. Some contracts include long terms, volume minimums, or early termination fees. The answer isn't to avoid factoring all of your loads. It's to know exactly what you're signing and work with a provider that's upfront about its terms.


## **Frequently Asked Questions**


### **Do I Have to Factor Every Load?**


It depends on your agreement and your provider. Many factoring agreements are built around submitting all eligible invoices. For most owner-operators and small fleets, factoring every load provides steadier cash flow and simpler operations.


### **What Is Spot Factoring?**


Spot factoring lets you factor individual invoices one at a time, usually with no ongoing agreement. It typically comes with higher rates, and works mostly for occasional, one-time cash needs.


### **What Is Selective Factoring?**


Selective factoring means choosing which invoices or brokers to factor. It sounds flexible, but it often adds paperwork, uneven cash flow, and more collections work for you.


### **Can I Factor Only Certain Loads?**


Some providers allow it, but terms vary by agreement and by broker. Factoring only certain loads usually means managing two systems and paying higher rates per invoice. Most carriers get more consistency by factoring all loads.


### **Is Factoring a Loan?**


No. Factoring is usually the sale of your unpaid invoices, not a traditional loan. You're turning completed work into working capital.


### **Can I Use Two Factoring Companies at the Same Time?**


Usually not. Most factoring agreements require exclusivity and include a UCC lien on your invoices. That generally prevents you from working with two factoring companies at once.


### **What's the Difference Between Recourse and Non-Recourse Factoring?**


With recourse factoring, you may have to buy back an invoice if the broker doesn't pay. With non-recourse factoring, the factoring company absorbs that loss if a broker goes out of business and can't pay—under the specific conditions outlined in your agreement. Read your contract to see what's covered.


### **Should New Owner-Operators Factor All Loads?**


In many cases, it can be a good idea. Cash reserves are usually thinnest in your first months of authority. Factoring every load keeps cash moving and gives you a credit check on every broker while you build your customer list.


### **How Do I Know What My Factoring Agreement Requires?**


Check your contract for volume requirements, fees, reserves, contract length, and exclusivity terms. A contract review with a factoring specialist can walk you through it line by line.


## **Get a Clear Look at Your Agreement**
